## 1. What you'll build, and why

Concept 21 gave you one way to write code against a protocol: the existential, `any Shape` — a
box holding *some unknown conformer*. Generics are the **other** way:

```swift
func pick<T: Shape>(_ a: T, _ b: T) -> T { ... }
```

Here `T` is not a box — it's a **type parameter**: unknown to the function, but *statically
consistent*. Both arguments are the *same* `T`; the result is that same `T` too, so the caller
gets back exactly what it put in (`pick(c1, c2).r` works — try that with `any Shape`!). This
concept builds generic functions end to end: the syntax, the call-site **inference**, the
constraint checking, and the runtime model — which turns out to reuse almost everything you built
for existentials, on purpose.

- **You implement:** the call-site inference (sema) and the call lowering (silgen).
- **Outcome:** generic programs run — matching swiftc, including under `-O`.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Static identity: what `T` adds over `any P`

An existential erases the type *per value*; a type parameter erases it *per call*, keeping
identity. Three consequences, all checkable statically:

1. `pick(A(x:3), B())` is an error — `conflicting arguments to generic parameter 'T' ('A' vs.
   'B')`. With `any P` parameters it would be fine (each box is independent).
2. The return type `T` *substitutes*: at `pick(A(x:3), A(x:8))`, the result IS an `A` — fields
   and all. An `any P` result would expose only `P`'s requirements forever.
3. Inside the body, `T` is opaque-but-constrained: `a.v()` is allowed because `T: P` and `v` is
   a requirement; `a.w()` is `value of type 'T' has no member 'w'` even if every conformer has a
   `w` — the *constraint* is the whole interface. That's the difference between Swift generics
   and C++ templates: a generic body is checked **once, against the constraint**, not per
   instantiation. (No SFINAE, no post-instantiation error novels.)

### Inference: the call site solves for T

There's no `pick<Circle>(...)` spelling needed — `T` is inferred from the arguments. The
algorithm you'll implement is the smallest real unifier:

- walk parameters and arguments together; every parameter typed `T` *binds* `T` to its
  argument's type — the first binding wins, later ones must **agree**;
- each binding must **satisfy its constraint** (`struct_conforms` from concept 21 — the same
  predicate, third customer);
- the declared return type has the bindings **substituted** in.

swiftc's version of this is the constraint solver (`CSGen`/`CSSolver`) — ours is the degenerate
single-variable case, but the shape (collect constraints, solve, substitute) is the same.

### The runtime model: one copy, erased to the constraint

How does *one* compiled function body handle every conformer? The answer this concept teaches —
and the reason 21 came first — is **erasure**:

![The unspecialized lowering: one compiled copy of `pick`, with `T` erased to its constraint's existential. The call site wraps concrete arguments (`init_existential`) and opens the `T`-result back to the statically-known type (`open_existential`). The body's `a.v()` is witness dispatch — it was compiled not knowing `T`.](figs/erasure.png)

Inside the compiled body, a `T` value *is* an `any P` — same `{payload, witness-table}` pair,
same dispatch. What's new is the **call boundary**:

- **wrap**: each argument in a `T` position gets `init_existential` (a concrete `A` becomes the
  pair; a value that's already erased — a generic calling a generic — passes through untouched);
- **open**: if the declared result is `T` and the caller inferred `T = A`, the call's result is
  `open_existential`-ed back to `$A` — a *statically checked* unwrap. No tag test, no trap: the
  type system proved the payload is an `A`, because the only way an `A`-bound call returns is
  with a `T` that *is* `A`. (swiftc spells this `open_existential` + an unchecked take.)

This is faithfully swiftc's **unspecialized** path (its generic ABI passes values indirectly
plus witness tables as hidden arguments — our existential rep is that, packaged). It's also
deliberately the *slow* path: every call wraps, every method inside is dynamic, and the inliner
is walled off. Concept 24 is the payoff: **specialization** clones `pick` per concrete type,
turning every `T` into `A`, every witness dispatch into a direct call, and feeding the whole
Phase-4 cascade. You're building the baseline it beats.

### The subset you are growing into

**New lexemes.** One keyword; the angle brackets are the comparison operators, reused:

| spelling | token | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `where` | `Token.Kw_where` | a keyword, in `token.ml`'s `keyword_or_ident` |
| `<` `>` in a signature | `Token.Lt` / `Token.Gt` | not new tokens — the parser reads a generic parameter list only in the one position it can occur, right after a `func` name, so there is no ambiguity with `a < b` to resolve |

**The grammar** — `<-- new` marks what this concept adds; everything else is concepts 05–21.
Notation is EBNF: `[ x ]` is *optional* (zero or one), `{ x }` is *repetition* (zero or more),
`|` separates alternatives, and quoted text is a terminal.

```
func_decl   ::= "func" ident [ generics ]                        <-- generics is new
                  "(" [ param { "," param } ] ")" [ "->" type ]
                  [ where_clause ] block                         <-- where_clause is new

generics    ::= "<" gparam { "," gparam } ">"                    <-- new
gparam      ::= ident ":" ident                                  <-- new  (T : P; v0 needs
                                                          the constraint, see below)
where_clause ::= "where" gparam { "," gparam }                   <-- new  (the same pairs,
                                                          spelled after the signature)

type        ::= [ "any" ] ident [ "?" ]
                (ident = a builtin, a struct, an enum, a protocol,
                       | a TYPE PARAMETER of the enclosing func)  <-- new
```

Two things to notice. `<T: P>` and `where T: P` produce the *same* list — the parser merges the
where-clause into `generics`, so nothing downstream has to know which spelling was used. And a
type parameter is only a type *inside its own function*: `resolve_opt` looks it up in
`current_generics`, which is pushed while checking that function's signature and body and popped
after, so `T` at top level is still `cannot find type 'T' in scope`.

### The diagnostics you emit

`infer_generic_call` is the first four rows; the rest are given, and `sema-inference.t` /
`sema-subset.t` keep them all on record. Wording follows `swiftc -typecheck` where the subset
lets it (`swift/include/swift/AST/DiagnosticsSema.def`, line numbers from the pinned snapshot).

| program | our message | swiftc |
|---|---|---|
| `pair(A(), B())` for `<T: P>(_: T, _: T)` | `conflicting arguments to generic parameter 'T' ('A' vs. 'B')` | **same** (`conflicting_arguments_for_generic_parameter`, l.415) |
| `one(D())` for `<T: P>` and a non-conformer `D` | `global function 'one' requires that 'D' conform to 'P'` | **same** (`type_does_not_conform_decl_owner`, l.2997 — `%kind0` prints as `global function 'one'`) |
| `one(3)` for `<T: P>` | `global function 'one' requires that 'Int' conform to 'P'` | **same** |
| `one(A(), A())` for a one-parameter `<T: P>` | `function 'one' expects 1 argument(s) but 2 given` | `extra argument in call` (`extra_argument_positional`, l.1696) — same verdict, and we keep the count-based sentence the rest of the compiler already uses |
| `a.w()` on a `T: P` where `w` is A's, not P's | `value of type 'T' has no member 'w'` | **same** (`could_not_find_value_member`, l.71) — the *constraint* is the whole interface |
| `a == b` on two `T` | `binary operator '==' cannot be applied to two 'T' operands` | **same** (`cannot_apply_binop_to_same_args`, l.221) |
| `func f<T>(_ a: T) -> T` | `type parameter 'T' needs a protocol constraint in this subset (write '<T: SomeProtocol>')` | **accepted** — swiftc has runtime type metadata for the unconstrained case; we have none yet, so we refuse the declaration. Our own words, deliberately: there is no swiftc sentence to copy |
| `one(e)` for `e: any P` and `<T: P>` | `global function 'one' requires that 'any P' conform to 'P'` | **accepted** — Swift 5.7 *opens* the existential implicitly (SE-0352) and binds `T` to the dynamic type. We cannot recover that type, so we refuse; the workaround is to keep the value concrete |

### Why v0 requires a constraint

`func ident<T>(_ x: T) -> T` is legal Swift — but with no constraint there's no witness table
and, more fundamentally, no *size*: our erased representation borrows the constraint's
existential buffer. swiftc solves this with runtime **type metadata** (every type, even `Int`,
has a metadata record carrying size/alignment/copy functions — that's the "value witness table",
concept 23's subject). We don't have metadata yet, so v0 rejects unconstrained parameters with a
clear message. The exercise sketches the metadata route.

> Oracle: `swift/docs/Generics.rst` is the canonical design document; `CSGen.cpp` for inference;
> the indirect calling convention is in `swift/lib/SILGen` (emitApply, indirect parameters).

## 3. Build it, step by step

Two holes, one per side of the call boundary. The sema one first: nothing lowers until the call
typechecks.

1. **`sema.ml` — `infer_generic_call`** (`TODO(22-sema)`). You are handed the callee's name, its
   `(type parameter, constraint)` list, its parameter types (which may mention `TVar`), its
   declared return, and the argument expressions. Produce the call's type, and report the four
   §2 diagnostics on the way. The shape is: check the arity; then walk parameters and arguments
   together, *inferring* at a `TVar` position and *checking* everywhere else; then hold each
   inferred binding up against its constraint (`struct_conforms`, from concept 21 — this is its
   third customer); then substitute into the declared return, so a `-> T` call has a concrete
   type at the caller. A binding that is itself a `TVar` with the same constraint is a generic
   calling a generic — it already satisfies the constraint, and there is nothing to substitute.
2. **`silgen.ml` — the call lowering** (`TODO(22-silgen)`, the `gfuncs` arm of `Ast.Call`). The
   callee is compiled ONCE with every `T` erased to `any P`, so this side does the boundary
   work. Lower each argument; the ones in a `TVar` position have to arrive as existentials, and
   `vty b v` tells you whether one already is. Apply the single erased copy — remember its
   result type is the *erased* return, so a `-> T` callee returns `$any P` here. Then, when the
   declared return is a `TVar` and the type you inferred for it is a concrete struct, open the
   result back to that struct: `Sil.Open_existential` is the statically-checked unwrap, and it
   is what makes `id(A(x: 8)).x` legal in the caller.

Tips. Inference happens twice, once in each hole — sema's binding does not travel to SILGen, so
the lowering re-derives it from the argument types it just lowered. Keep the two consistent or
the open will name a type the payload does not hold. Everything else is given: parsing
`<T: P>` and `where`, the `TVar` scoping, the erased lowering of the generic function itself,
and IRGen's `open_existential`.

Reference: `solution/sema.ml`, `solution/silgen.ml`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase5-generics/22-generics                       # everything
make lab C=phase5-generics/22-generics T=sema-inference      # one hole
```

One cram file per hole, in fill order:

| file | goes green when | how it checks |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/sema-inference.t` | `TODO(22-sema)` infers | `--typecheck`: a substituted `-> T` result used concretely, and the conflict / constraint / arity refusals of §2 with their positions |
| `tests/silgen-generic-call.t` | `TODO(22-silgen)` lowers the call | `--emit-sil` for the shapes (ONE `@first` with an `$any P` signature; `init_existential` in, `open_existential` out; neither for a generic calling a generic), then the programs **run**, at `-Onone` and `-O` |

Two files do not belong to a hole. `tests/sema-subset.t` is GIVEN code and green from the start:
the aggregate refusals carried in from phase 3, plus this concept's three body rules — a member
that is not in the constraint, `==` on two `T`s, and the unconstrained `<T>` v0 refuses. None of
them involves a *call*, which is why they work before `infer_generic_call` exists. And
`tests/oracle.t` is the headline: 22 programs of `typecheck-corpus.txt` where `swiftc -typecheck`
and `--typecheck` must reach the same verdict, then 18 of `oracle-corpus.txt` compiled **four
ways** — `swiftc -Onone`, `swiftc -O`, `./lab.exe build`, `./lab.exe build -O` — all run, stdout
and exit code identical.

`make lab` distinguishes three kinds of red. **TODO** means nothing in that file passes — the
hole has not been started, and the file just lists what it will check. **FAIL** means *some*
cases pass: you are mid-hole, and the diffs are worth reading (`DETAIL=1` shows them). **SKIP**
means a compile error stopped dune before the file ran. On the untouched skeleton both holes'
files read TODO, `sema-subset.t` reads PASS, and the alcotest suite reads FAIL — its `body`
group is green from the start, its `inference` and `lowering` groups are not.

## 5. Benchmark it

Time `apply3(Inc(by: 5), x)` in a hot loop against a hand-monomorphized version: the generic
pays wrap + dynamic dispatch per call and blocks inlining. Hold that number — concept 24's
specializer should close the gap to zero, and *measuring the gap now* is what makes 24's gate
meaningful.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Multiple type parameters.** `func zip2<A: P, B: Q>(_ a: A, _ b: B) -> Int` — the inference
   generalizes to a per-parameter binding map; conflicts stay per-parameter.
2. **Unconstrained `T` via boxing.** Give every type a minimal metadata record (size in words)
   and represent unconstrained `T` as `{ [K x i64], ptr metadata }`; reject types over K words.
   You've just invented the value-witness direction concept 23 completes.
3. **Generic methods.** `func scaled<T: Factor>(_ by: T) -> Int` inside a struct — the method's
   generics compose with `self`; the lowering adds the erased parameter after `self`.
4. **Explicit specialization, by hand.** Write `pick_A` (the monomorphized clone) yourself and
   diff its SIL against the generic's — you're previewing exactly what concept 24 automates.

## 7. Recap & what's next

A type parameter is a *statically consistent* unknown: inferred per call, checked against its
constraint once, erased to the constraint's existential in the one compiled copy — wrap going
in, open coming out. Generics and existentials share a runtime model; they differ in what the
*type system* knows, and that static knowledge is unexploited fuel.

Next, **23-existentials** goes deeper into the box itself — what happens when values outgrow
the inline buffer (heap boxing), how copies/destroys work for an unknown type (**value witness
tables**), and `as?` opening. Then **24-specialization** burns the static fuel: clone,
devirtualize, inline, and watch the Phase-4 pipeline erase the entire abstraction cost.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
(* sema: the inference *)
and infer_generic_call f generics ptypes ret (args : Ast.arg list) span : Types.ty =
  let exprs = List.map snd args in
  let np = List.length ptypes and na = List.length exprs in
  if np <> na then (
    err span (Printf.sprintf "function '%s' expects %d argument(s) but %d given" f np na);
    ret)
  else begin
    let bind = ref [] in
    List.iter2
      (fun pt a ->
        match pt with
        | Types.TVar (n, _) -> (
            let t = infer a in
            match List.assoc_opt n !bind with
            | None -> bind := (n, t) :: !bind
            | Some t0 ->
                if not (Types.equal t0 t) then
                  err span (Printf.sprintf
                    "conflicting arguments to generic parameter '%s' ('%s' vs. '%s')"
                    n (Types.string_of_ty t0) (Types.string_of_ty t)))
        | _ -> check_expr a pt)
      ptypes exprs;
    List.iter
      (fun (n, c) ->
        match List.assoc_opt n !bind with
        | Some (Types.TStruct sn) ->
            if not (struct_conforms sn c) then
              err span
                (Printf.sprintf "global function '%s' requires that '%s' conform to '%s'"
                   f sn c)
        | Some (Types.TVar (_, c')) when c' = c -> ()
        | Some t ->
            err span
              (Printf.sprintf "global function '%s' requires that '%s' conform to '%s'"
                 f (Types.string_of_ty t) c)
        | None -> ())
      generics;
    match ret with
    | Types.TVar (n, _) -> ( match List.assoc_opt n !bind with Some t -> t | None -> ret)
    | t -> t
  end

(* silgen: the call lowering *)
else if Hashtbl.mem b.gfuncs f then (
  let _, ptypes, ret = Hashtbl.find b.gfuncs f in
  let binding = ref [] in
  let argvs =
    List.map2
      (fun pt (_, e) ->
        match pt with
        | Types.TVar (n, c) -> (
            let v = gen_expr b e in
            if not (List.mem_assoc n !binding) then binding := (n, vty b v) :: !binding;
            match vty b v with
            | Types.TProto _ -> v
            | Types.TStruct sn -> emit b (Sil.Init_existential (v, sn, c)) (Types.TProto c)
            | _ -> assert false)
        | _ -> gen_expr_as b e pt)
      ptypes args
  in
  let erased_ret = match ret with Types.TVar (_, c) -> Types.TProto c | t -> t in
  let fr = emit b (Sil.Func_ref f) erased_ret in
  let callv = emit b (Sil.Apply (fr, argvs)) erased_ret in
  match ret with
  | Types.TVar (n, _) -> (
      match List.assoc_opt n !binding with
      | Some (Types.TStruct sn) ->
          emit b (Sil.Open_existential (callv, sn)) (Types.TStruct sn)
      | _ -> callv)
  | _ -> callv)
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — multiple type parameters

The `bind` map already keys by parameter name; nothing changes in the algorithm — only the
conformance pass iterates all of `generics`. The interesting new error is a return type
mentioning an *unbound* parameter (no argument position used it): swiftc rejects the
declaration ("generic parameter 'B' is not used in function signature" appears when it's used
nowhere; if used only in the return, inference fails at the call) — pick the declaration-time
check, it's kinder.

### 2 — unconstrained T

Metadata-lite: emit one global per struct `@meta.S = { i64 words }` and represent unconstrained
`T` as `{ [K x i64], ptr }` where the ptr is metadata instead of a witness table. Copies inside
the generic body are bitwise (fine for our value types — no ARC yet), so the only metadata
consumer is the open at the call boundary. The deep version — copy/destroy function pointers in
the metadata — is the value witness table, concept 23.

### 3 — generic methods

Parse generics after the method name; the method's `gfuncs` entry includes `self`'s concrete
type as parameter 0 (not erased — `self` is known!). Lowering: `S.m` takes `(%S, any P, ...)`.
Dispatch on a generic method through a *protocol requirement* is where this gets deep (witness
thunks per instantiation) — out of scope until specialization exists.

### 4 — by-hand specialization

`func pick_A(_ a: A, _ b: A) -> A` compiles to direct calls on `%A` values — no
`init_existential`, no `witness_method`, and after `-O` the comparisons inline to field reads.
Diff `--sil-opt` outputs: every line that differs is a line concept 24 will delete
automatically.
```
